title: There Is No Harm in Stopping for an Hour
intro: Abu Tammam addresses Ahmad, son of the caliph al-Mu'tasim. At the abandoned camp a woman asks to be remembered, and the lover’s sense of obligation becomes the petitioner’s hope in the Abbasids. Having likened Ahmad to four famous men, the poet defends the use of a lesser thing to describe a greater one by recalling the Qur’anic likeness of the light.

translation: There is no harm in stopping for an hour.
Let us pay what we owe the worn-out camps.
1.sharh: An “hour” is a while on the road. A slight delay for one traveller will allow two of them to discharge a debt to people who are no longer there to receive it.

translation: Perhaps your eye will help with water of its own.
Some tears desert a man, others stand by him.
2.sharh: The companion can add his tears to the lover’s. Tears themselves are assigned two human characters, the friend who fails to appear and the friend who stays.

translation: No drowsy lover can console the one who longs,
dry at the eyes, cool of breath.
3.sharh: To “help” a mourner can mean to weep alongside him. The dry eyes and cool breath diagnose a passion too sleepy to offer that particular help.

translation: Parting sprang upon these dwellings
and emptied every gazelle’s lair of its white gazelles,
4.sharh: Parting pounces like an animal. The empty lair is a gazelle’s scraped-out resting place and also a way of seeing the abandoned homes of the departing women.

translation: women bright across the breast, finely fashioned
as the slender shoot of a swaying ban tree.
5.sharh: “Laughing” belongs to her upper chest in Arabic, where the expression makes the skin shine. The long flexible shoot supplies the movement of a living figure.

translation: A full moon, she yielded all too readily to sudden departure,
a sun with a passion for keeping clear of you.
6.sharh: Her beauty fills the sky, yet she proves eager to leave and hard to approach. The Arabic for the sun, shams, almost reappears in shimas, the skittishness of a restive mount.

translation: A young woman whose smile flashes
like white chamomile flowering in sandy earth.
7.sharh: The smile reveals small separate patches of white. The sandy setting gives the chamomile a background against which its petals stand out as the teeth do.

translation: When she walks she leaves your breast twice as full
of whispers as the ornaments she wears.
8.sharh: One Arabic word does double duty for the whisper of jewellery and inward, recurring thoughts. Her footfall ends long before the disturbance it sets going in the observer.

translation: She spoke when our parting was decreed, its cup
having bewildered the one who poured and the one who drank.
9.sharh: A cup normally works on the drinker. This one overcomes the server too, so that both parties to the farewell can be heard in the woman’s anxiety.

translation: “Do not forget those promises. You were only
called insan, human, because you forget.”
10.sharh: Insan, the Arabic word for a human being, sounds close to words for forgetting. She turns a disputed old etymology into a lover’s pointed reminder to keep faith.

translation: He who created all creatures has appointed
their means of life through the changing ages.
11.sharh: The move from farewell to patronage begins at the widest possible scale. Creation implies continuing provision, and the next verse specifies where a petitioner might look for his share.

translation: The earth receives the sky’s kindness as a guest’s meal.
Those who live in hope have the sons of Abbas.
12.sharh: Rain is the hospitality the sky extends to the earth. The parallel recasts men who seek a ruler’s favour as an entire family, the figurative “sons of hope.”

translation: These men are God’s shade. He lodged His faith
among them. They are the mountain where kings stand firm.
13.sharh: Shade suggests shelter in the sun, the mountain an enduring support. Both pictures magnify the dynasty before Ahmad is singled out by name.

translation: Every jewel has a gleaming lustre.
They are the lustre of all these people.
14.sharh: Firind can be the sheen that discloses the quality of a polished object. The praise locates the people’s distinction in the dynasty just as a gem’s worth shows in the light playing on it.

translation: My restless purpose settled on hope of Ahmad.
Report and reasoning alike circled back to him,
15.sharh: Following received authority and reasoning by analogy are distinct ways of reaching a judgment. The poet makes both arrive at the same door and puts his wandering ambition at rest.

translation: the chosen, the elect, the picked man
for praise, adorned with it and clothing others in it.
16.sharh: Three words for selection keep narrowing the choice to Ahmad. He both wears praise as an ornament and has it in his power to confer distinction on somebody else.

translation: Praise is a beautiful mantle in which
the finest deeds walk proud. No loom made that cloak.
17.sharh: The handsome deeds become wearers, strutting in the fine fabric of a good name. Calling it a mantle “of clothing” at the end briefly puts a real garment beside the imagined one.

translation: A shoot of Hashim grew in soil
for which he was a fitting plant.
18.sharh: Hashim names an ancestor and, through him, the family’s good soil. A fine lineage still needs an individual plant capable of doing it justice.

translation: The rains never forsake its growing place.
Even the heart of the hard ground has no hardness for it.
19.sharh: Hardness moves from soil texture to human feeling. Even a patch of tough ground softens towards this particular planting when rain reaches it.

translation: As if the two had suckled at one breast,
so close their friendship, or nursed at the same cup.
20.sharh: A shared breast makes foster siblings, and a shared cup makes drinking companions. The immediate pair is plant and soil. Commentators also take it as Ahmad and the praise that suits him.

translation: His bloom is the bloom of arar, his breath
the scent of lavender in the green of myrtle.
21.sharh: Each plant contributes a different quality. Flower and perfume give immediate pleasure, while the evergreen myrtle contributes something that lasts beyond one flowering.

translation: You have endowed this glory with the furthest reach
of ambition, the noblest character and stock,
22.sharh: Glory itself is made the recipient of a gift. The turn to “you” credits Ahmad with extending what glory can mean, before the poet names the men by whom a listener can measure it.

translation: Amr’s daring joined to Hatim’s open hand,
Ahnaf’s forbearance to Iyas’s quick wit.
23.sharh: Each name was proverbial for a single excellence. The repeated “in” of the Arabic nests daring, liberality, restraint and intelligence in a single person.

translation: Do not fault me for choosing men beneath him
to make a far-travelling comparison for bounty and valour.
24.sharh: The comparisons must use men the audience already knows. Calling the saying a wanderer makes its readiness to travel part of the poet’s defence.

translation: God Himself chose something lesser for His light,
a likeness drawn from a niche and a lamp.
25.sharh: In the Light Verse, the reader is asked to picture a lamp set in a niche. Abu Tammam draws on that familiar image to answer his critics. A comparison can help people understand something greater than itself.

translation: If you win glory’s prize in the first flush of youth,
son of the caliph, Abu al-Abbas,
26.sharh: A prize belongs to the winner of a contest. The prince’s youth might make such an early win surprising, and his family name prepares the answer that follows.

translation: many a fire of yours has been brought to life
in the night from a single borrowed flame.
27.sharh: A traveller needs only a little live fire to kindle a blaze visible in the dark. Ahmad’s early gifts have the capacity of that small flame in a family accustomed to lighting fires.

translation: Many a poor rider in a crisis you have made
sit fast through its worst, fast as a saddlecloth.
28.sharh: The Arabic moves from a rider who cannot keep his seat to the cloth that never leaves the saddle. Ahmad’s help has changed another man’s ability to face trouble.

translation: You sustained him in poverty, that wasting illness,
with generosity, the physician who heals.
29.sharh: The internal illness is the hidden damage poverty does. Giving works like a physician because it reaches the cause of the man’s debility.

translation: You have made him so at home with time itself
he takes it for a wedding feast.
30.sharh: Time in the ode is ordinarily an unreliable host. Help with a real privation has changed the man’s experience of it so completely that daily life resembles a wedding celebration.

translation: Joy has mastered my worries through
the kindness and welcome you have shown me.
31.sharh: The beneficiary suddenly has a first-person voice. The separate gifts of support and companionship answer the loneliness that first made him ask a fellow traveller to stop.

translation: Grey hair turned on my youth before its time.
Age did not send it. Despair did.
32.sharh: Despair had left the visible sign normally reserved for age. The line explains why relief from a patron can enter an account of what has happened to the speaker’s hair.

translation: The mark of what we seek is on the heart.
The years impress their brand upon the head.
33.sharh: A brand is a mark that remains legible to others. The distinction between head and heart explains the previous surprise, when an inward disappointment appeared on his head.

translation: Only now have I planted in generous soil
those hopes of mine, and built on a foundation.
34.sharh: The good soil that grew the prince can now receive the speaker’s hopes. The final building has a foundation, answering the first sight of abandoned, crumbling homes.

1.2.2.head: ذِمام
1.2.2.meaning: A claim of loyalty which it would be shameful to neglect.

1.2.3-4.head: الأَربُع الأَدراس
1.2.3-4.meaning: Old stopping places whose traces have worn away.

2.1.4.head: أَعانَ
2.1.4.meaning: To lend assistance, here to join in weeping.

3.1.1-2.head: أَسعَدَ
3.1.1-2.meaning: To lend another mourner the support of one’s own tears.

3.1.4.head: وَسنان
3.1.4.meaning: Drowsy, as if the man’s capacity to love had dozed off.

4.2.3.head: آرام
4.2.3.meaning: White gazelles. In the abandoned camp they evoke the women who once lived there.

4.2.5.head: كِناس
4.2.5.meaning: A hollow scraped out by a gazelle for shelter.

5.1.4.head: التَّرائِب
5.1.4.meaning: The upper chest or collarbone area.

6.1.4.head: بادِرَة
6.1.4.meaning: A sudden onset, here the abrupt arrival of separation.

6.2.4.head: شِماس
6.2.4.meaning: Restiveness or shying away, originally of an animal.

7.2.1-2.head: نَور الأَقاحي
7.2.1-2.meaning: The white flowers of chamomile or a similar daisy.

8.2.1.head: حُليّ
8.2.1.meaning: Jewellery such as bracelets, heard here when its wearer moves.

8.2.4.head: الوَسواس
8.2.4.meaning: A faint rustle, also an inward whisper or recurring thought.

9.1.3.meaning: To be decreed or become inevitable.

11.1.5.head: قاتَ
11.1.5.meaning: To provide creatures with what keeps them alive. The Arabic verb and the word for provisions in the next half have the same root.

11.2.3.head: الأَحراس
11.2.3.meaning: Long stretches of time, not the ordinary sense of guards.

12.1.4.head: قِرى
12.1.4.meaning: Hospitality in the form of a meal or provision.

14.1.4.head: فِرِند
14.1.4.meaning: Firind, the brilliant sheen of a gem or blade, a Persian loanword.

15.1.4.head: أَحمَد
15.1.4.meaning: Ahmad ibn al-Mu'tasim, the caliph’s son, addressed as Abu al-Abbas.

15.2.4.head: قِياس
15.2.4.meaning: Reasoning by analogy, paired here with relying on another person’s judgement.

16.1.3.head: المُستَرى
16.1.3.meaning: One chosen from the best. Al-A'lam reads “the buyer of praise”, a man who spends his wealth and earns people’s commendation.

17.1.2.head: بُرد
17.1.2.meaning: A woven, often figured or striped mantle.

17.2.1-2.head: غُرَر الفَعال
17.2.1-2.meaning: “The finest of deeds.” He imagines those deeds as people walking proudly in the mantle of praise.

18.1.4.head: هاشِم
18.1.4.meaning: Hashim ibn Abd Manaf, the ancestor after whom the Hashimites take their name.

19.1.3.head: الأَنواء
19.1.3.meaning: Star-marked weather seasons, here the rains they bring.

21.1.2.head: العَرارَة
21.1.2.meaning: Arar, a fragrant flowering herb, singled out here for its bloom.

21.2.2.meaning: Lavender, supplying the fragrance of the imagined tree.

21.2.5.head: الآس
21.2.5.meaning: Myrtle, an evergreen shrub whose green supplies the colour in the comparison.

23.1.2.head: عَمرٌو
23.1.2.meaning: Amr ibn Ma'dikarib, the warrior proverbial for taking the lead in danger.

23.1.5.head: حاتِم
23.1.5.meaning: Hatim of Tayy, proverbial for open-handed hospitality.

23.2.3.head: أَحنَف
23.2.3.meaning: Al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, a Tamim leader famed for forbearance.

23.2.6.head: إِياس
23.2.6.meaning: Iyas ibn Mu'awiya, a Basra judge famed for quick perception.

24.2.2.head: شَرود
24.2.2.meaning: Far-ranging, of a saying that travels on people’s tongues.

25.2.3.head: المِشكاة
25.2.3.meaning: Mishkat, the lamp niche in Qur’an 24.35.

26.1.3.head: خَصل
26.1.3.meaning: The stake or prize of a contest.

26.1.6-7.head: أَنف الصِّبا
26.1.6-7.meaning: “The forepart of youth”, its beginnings, when a person is still very young.

27.2.4.head: قَبَس
27.2.4.meaning: A flame taken from one fire to kindle another. The fire that lights the night starts from this small gift.

28.1.2.head: كِفل
28.1.2.meaning: An unsteady rider liable to fall off.

28.2.2.head: حِلس
28.2.2.meaning: A saddlecloth which stays against the animal’s back.

29.1.3.head: العُدم
29.1.3.meaning: Poverty or want. At the end of the half-line the poet gives this lack of means the name of an illness.

29.2.4.meaning: A healer who tends an injury or illness.

33.2.3.head: وَسم
33.2.3.meaning: A lasting brand or impressed mark.
